Elements of this aesthetic are heavily tied to its roots in mimicking vintage photos of the late 1800s/early 1900s, which often had a heavy, dirty gradient quality due to its limited excess technology. During the late 1980s, there was a steady rise of indie artists that included a lot of vintage low quality vibes in their music videos. This contrasted with the rise of grunge and then affected the rest of the 1990s. This ode to vintage styles can also be seen in the rise of aesthetics such as
. Sepia Blur uses desaturated colors and grainy/worn out filters, especially in promotional materials and music videos.

When grunge music exploded onto the global stage in the early 1990s, it brought more than a new sound. It reshaped the entire visual culture of popular music. Music videos, once dominated by glamour, excess, and idealized imagery, began to mirror the raw, emotional honesty of the Seattle-based movement. What emerged was a gritty, unpolished visual language that rejected the artificiality of the previous decade. Indie acts of the late 1980s were already moving away from the access glamour and spectacle of the 80s that continued to persist with trends such as

The Jangle Pop craze, which was a brief callback to the 1960s and early 1970s, had a heavy emphasis on its usage of grainy and off-filtered aesthetics; this was likely the first sign of the sepia blur aesthetic, as singer-songwriter Tracy Chapman's cover from her 1988 self-titled debut album was a picture of her with sepia-toned layering and vintage grain reminiscent of old pictures from the early 1900s as discussed earlier. The 1980s music scene itself wasn't oblivious to vintage aesthetics used in either music videos or album covers. Many paid lip service to it, but it wouldn't hit its stride until the late 1980s indie scene and of course grunge.

Sepia Blur was dominated by heavy sepia browns, greys, and muted oranges. It often features "decaying" visuals like heavy film grain, light leaks, and blurry, off-focus imagery. It was a bridge between the
. The music videos often included film flashing that was meant to mimic an old film reel. Notice the heavy film grain and "noise" across the lit side of the face. This
rejects the slick, airbrushed style of late 80s/early 90s

90s Sepia was often used in advertising, especially for adult-targeted campaigns, such as technology, fashion, interior design, and healthy lifestyle. The colors often used in advertising of the 90s is either sepia brown, heathered grey (the biggest examples being ads from Calvin Klein). For industries like

, these tones were used to humanize cold products. A sleek computer or a piece of furniture wasn't just a machine or an object; when bathed in sepia or set against heathered textures, it felt like part of a warm, lived-in lifestyle. This "new neutral" look suggested that the consumer was mature, discerning, and valued quality over flashiness.

After grunge quickly rose to prominence in the mainstream, many corporations quickly capitalized on its success, especially among the youth. This led to corporations using deem shading and David Carson-style iconography for products unrelated to grunge; this aesthetic is widely known as

. Ultimately, Corporate Grunge was a way to market to Generation X by adopting their cynical, anti-establishment posture. By using "shredded" graphics and muted, heathered tones, a corporation could pretend it wasn't a corporation at all—it was just another "outsider." This aesthetic eventually paved the way for the
look, as the "gritty" textures of grunge began to merge with the sleek, digital optimism of the coming millennium.

c: With the rise of grunge and GVC in the 1990s, many TV shows, commercials, and movies showcased and/or contained very desaturated, grainy, and sepia-styled tones; these were either a stylized choice or meant to convey the aesthetic direction the 1990s had taken at that time. Shows like
contained low-contrast palettes. In the case of
, it was due to the subject matter it tackled, while

was often due to where it was set. The lighting was often warm but dimmed, using amber lamps to create a sepia-adjacent glow. This conveyed a sense of intellectualism and "old-world" comfort in a modern Seattle setting.

For commercials, many went down the edgy pipeline, especially after the success of alt-rock in the mainstream. Not all commercials were grungy, however some went for a very soft and slick look, especially as old money/big tech aspects started to take hold. When it came to certain products like technological devices, beauty products, formal fashion, and healthy lifestyle, the commercials targeted a very adult audience by using heathered grey or sepia tone filtering to drive home this contrast. Commercials for brands like Levi’s or Nike began using "shaky cam" and bleached-out colors. By removing the vibrancy, these brands appeared more "honest." A desaturated, grainy athlete looked like they were working harder; a sepia-toned denim ad looked like a piece of history rather than a sales pitch.

Movies showcased this aesthetic as well, but only in specific genres, such as erotic thrillers, neo-noir films or crime dramas. The 1990s were no strangers to erotic thrillers, as there was a prominent trend of adult-oriented erotic thrillers that often paid homage to the suspense noir films of the 1930s and 1940s. These films would often be desaturated and sepia-toned. Examples include

(1992), which are just to name a few. These films functioned as a "bridge" between the classical suspense of Hitchcock and the cynical realism of the 90s. The use of sepia specifically evoked the look of aging photographs.

During the late 1980s, the sepia tone filter began to reach mainstream success with the popularity of indie-based jangle pop. While jangle pop brought a shimmering, 1960s-inspired "chime" to 80s and 90s indie music, its visual style used sepia tones and motion blur to signal nostalgia, DIY authenticity, and emotional vulnerability. Various bands such as The Smiths, The La's, The Sundays and R.E.M. used this aesthetic in many of their cover art. Once grunge fully entered mainstream consciousness, most indie and alternative rock bands switched to using grunge-based aesthetics and visuals. This look became the bridge to grunge. While jangle pop was "clean" and "sweet," the "Sepia Burning" variation added a darker, decaying edge. You see this evolution in the transition from the soft sepia of Tracy Chapman's debut to the grittier, blurred visuals of early 90s alternative acts like The Gin Blossoms or Teenage Fanclub, who kept the "jangle" but added the "grunge" dirt.

Another one of those genres would be shoegaze; bands in the shoegaze genre would pay heavy homage to the sixties-based psychedelic, even incorporating psychedelia on their album covers with a slight sepia-toned, blurred tint. Visuals often featured extreme close-ups of objects until they blurred into "amorphous blotches" of color and light. This reflected how individual instruments in a shoegaze track often blended into a single, massive texture.

From roughly the early 1990s and especially the mid 1990s, black musicians would incorporate heavy usages of sepia tones on their album covers, music videos and promotional material. This was because 1990s R&B entered into a more soulful direction that harkened back to its early roots; sepia was often the color of choice for R&B at the time and would even go into the new millennium. In R&B music videos, the sepia blur was the go-to aesthetic for slow jams. It was used to make the footage feel like a cinematic memory rather than a contemporary TV broadcast. Directors used "mist filters" to soften light and create a glow around artists, which, when combined with earth tones (tans, browns, and creams), gave videos a lush, expensive feel. The artists that often went for this style were Janet Jackson, TLC (especially during

Grunge's aesthetic was likely the reason for sepia blur becoming so widely influential throughout other genres of the 1990s. As the 1990s came into the fold, the tone of most music videos and promotional material for music felt very "grungy", whether it was pop, alt rock, indie or even dance music. Most of the videos feature a very dark, desaturated or muted color palette with grainy visuals. Grunge was the catalyst for the "anti-glamour" visual language of the 1990s. It rejected the neon, high-gloss finish of the 1980s in favor of something that felt "dirty," "real," and "human." Many alternative music videos of the era (like those for Nirvana or Alice in Chains) combined these gritty, sepia-toned images with dreamlike, out-of-focus imagery to create a "Grunge Surrealist" vibe that felt both raw and unsettling.
